docs.title: D95 vs. Company Item Engagement Analysis
docs.text: Skills: Excel SQL PowerPoint

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This project analyzes QR code engagement performance for department D95 compared to company-wide trends.

Goal: Understand QR engagement behavior, identify performance drivers, and provide actionable recommendations for content, placement, and timing.

All data displayed is simulated for demonstration purposes only.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Every data project starts with a question. Whether it emerges spontaneously in a meeting or stems from a defined business problem, meaningful data work is impossible without a guiding question or end outcome in mind. It will help understand what data to collect, prevent inefficient resource and time allocation, and enhance the effectiveness and relevance of insights. Without it, analyzing data becomes more like searching for a needle in a haystack.

  • How can we increase engagement?
  • Are shoppers interacting with PIP codes? If not, why?
  • How does D95 compare to the rest of the company?

docs.title: Clarifying the Business Questions
docs.text:
After clarifying the scope with stakeholders, the key questions became:

  • How did D95 perform during spring/summer compared to the company?
  • Are customers meaningfully engaging with PIP codes?
  • How can we optimize signage placement in stores to better grab audience's attention?

This helped define exactly which data to extract, enabling a more efficient workflow where:

  • Knew which data sources to use
  • Only relevant metrics were captured
  • No unnecessary data pulling

docs.title: 1. Data Collection
docs.text:
Rather than pulling full exports with every piece of data included, I collected only essential metrics from our internal Tableau dashboards:

  • Total unique scans
  • Items tracked
  • Visits per store per week (v/s/w)
  • Daily/weekly engagement trends

docs.title: 2. Data Cleaning & Preparation (SQL + Excel)
docs.text:
Using SQL, I created a CTE to extract YTD department-level and class-level performance. Data cleanup in SQL included:

  • Replacing/removing NULLs
  • Trimming whitespace
  • Converting date strings → datetime
  • Standardizing naming conventions

docs.title: 3. Exploratory & Comparative Analysis
docs.text:
I performed analysis using Excel and Tableau:

  • PivotTables
  • SUMIFs, IF, XLOOKUP, and sorting functions
  • Time-series exploration
  • Company vs. department comparisons

Key findings:

  • D95 outperformed the company in spring/summer, despite over 95% of D95 codes linking to PIP content, which are notorious for being oversaturated and low engagement.
  • Seasonal consumer behavior (home improvement during warm months) drove this higher engagement.
  • Certain page types (Collection, HD Program, Home Services) showed strong positive lifts.

docs.title: 4. Insight Delivery
docs.text:
I created a user-friendly PowerPoint report that included:

  • KPI summaries
  • Weekly trend charts
  • D95 vs. Company comparisons
  • Page-type performance tables
  • Clear callouts & recommendations

This enabled teams to:

  • Test content/copy for higher engagement
  • Optimize QR placement
  • Adjust campaign timing for relevance

docs.title: Business Impact
docs.text:
This analysis delivered several meaningful outcomes:

  • Improved targeting: Identified the top performing 20% of QR codes that drove 55% of total engagement, enabling more focused content and placement strategies.
  • PIP codes validated: Demonstrated that select PIP QR codes achieved 30-45% higher engagement during peak seasonal periods, disproving the assumption that PIP pages always underperform.
  • Benchmarking clarity: Showed that D95 outperformed the company-wide average by 12-18% during spring/summer, giving the team a clear benchmark for future comparison.
  • Optimized placement/timing: Found that relocating signage and aligning launches with seasonal peaks increased engagement by an estimated 15–20% compared to off-cycle deployments.

docs.title: Follow-Up Questions & Investigation
docs.text:
Every data project also probably ends with a question. After reviewing the findings, several additional questions came up that would help compile more in depth insights.

  • Which copy, visuals, or layouts drive higher engagement?
    • Recommendation: Controlled A/B testing to measure how copy, imagery, and layout variations influence engagement.
  • Do different store formats or regions respond uniquely to QR signage?
    • Recommendation: Break performance down by store format, region, and traffic patterns to tailor signage strategies.
  • Which in store locations (endcaps, aisles, service areas) generate the highest lift?
    • Recommendation: Run pilot tests in selected stores comparing different physical signage placements.
  • When should campaigns launch to best capture peak demand windows?
    • Recommendation: Use historical data to predict engagement windows and guide campaign planning for finding the right timing for the most impact.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This analysis demonstrated how targeted, well structured data can uncover meaningful insights that directly inform business decisions. By grounding the project in clear questions, focusing on essential metrics, and delivering findings in an understandable format, the team gained a deeper understanding of D95’s engagement performance and actionable steps. Ultimately, this project illustrates the value of using data to provide strategic guidance that influences business decisions.

docs.title: Process Optimization Test Benefits Overview
docs.text: Skills: Excel PowerPoint

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This project evaluated a process improvement pilot designed to reduce labor inefficiencies associated with SKU location tasks and digital loading delays. The objective was to determine the optimal threshold that delivers the strongest ROI without requiring universal store rollout. Through two controlled pilot store tests, the team identified a 25% adoption maximizes impact while minimizing cost.

All data displayed is simulated for demonstration purposes only.

docs.title: Key Callouts
docs.text:
• Updated signage and process adjustments reduced reliance on digital loading, resulting in a time saving of 28.4 seconds per task.
  • Company-wide benefits increased significantly for Pilot Store A, with Pilot Store B showing moderate improvement due to lower adoption and usage in participating stores.
  • A 25% implementation rate was identified as the feasible and highest ROI threshold, as 100% adoption is neither operationally or financially realistic.

docs.title: Business Impact
docs.text:
• $54.3M in total annualized labor savings
  • $36.2M in savings from Pilot Store A alone
  • $7.8M in savings from Pilot Store B
  • $10.3M in inventory savings, reducing errors that historically required manual rework.
  • Categories such as Hardware, Fasteners, and Safety generated the highest labor savings, indicating where implementation would be most impactful.
  • Provided leaders with clear, data-driven guidance on where to invest, allowing them to feel confident in the new implementation.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
• Implement in areas with the highest labor hours and strongest ROI (e.g., Hardware, Fasteners, Safety).
  • Use store-level operational data (SKU density, task volume, labor hours per week) to identify the most impactful locations.
  • Document a repeatable, simplified SOP to ensure the process can be implemented consistently across the feasible 25% of stores.
  • Invest in signage or digital tools only in stores that handle a high volume of relevant SKUs and maintain strong compliance. Avoid rolling out to low-benefit stores.

docs.title: Home Depot Simulated Supplier Insights Dashboard
docs.text:
Skills: Tableau Python Excel GitHub

Note: The dashboard experience is best viewed in fullscreen mode.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This project explores supplier performance using a simulated multi-year dataset built in Python. The analysis evaluates revenue, conversion rates, content quality, and product level behavior, uncovering insights to guide merchandising strategy, supplier management, and digital content optimization.

Goal: Identify performance drivers across suppliers and SKUs while quantifying opportunities for improved conversion, content quality, and customer engagement.

This dashboard was built using a simulated dataset generated in Python. The dataset is designed to reflect realistic COVID impacts, supplier behavior, and conversion patterns. The code used to generate the dataset can be found below.

View Python Code

docs.title: Guiding Questions
docs.text:
• Which suppliers contribute the most revenue?
  • How does content quality impact conversion?
  • Where are the biggest risks? Missing images, low conversion, or asset quality issues?
  • What actions can merchandising teams take to improve performance?

docs.title: Business Questions
docs.text:
• Which suppliers deliver the highest revenue, and how efficient are they (revenue per view)?
  • How do product page views translate into orders?
  • How large is the missing-image problem, and which brands are most affected?
  • How does content score correlate to conversion?
  • At the SKU level, which items carry the highest risk or greatest opportunity?

docs.title: Data Generation, Simulation Design, & Preparation
docs.text:
The dataset was designed to mimic:

  • COVID-era demand swings
  • Supplier-level behavior differences
  • Category-level seasonality
  • Conversion patterns across millions of views
  • Content quality variance (image completeness, asset quality, bullet quality)

Metrics collected include:

  • Revenue, orders, conversion rate
  • Page views & funnel step counts
  • Content score & asset quality score
  • Missing image flags
  • SKU metadata (supplier, category, product type)

NOTE: skip to Exploratory Analysis if you are not interested in how the dataset was generated and designed. It's a LONG section!!

docs.title: 1. Imports, Random Seed, and Core Dimensions
docs.text:
We start by importing libraries, fixing a random seed for reproducibility, and defining the size and dimensions of the dataset. A sample size of n = 200,000 was chosen to provide enough volume to model realistic retail behavior while staying relatively manageable for exploratory analysis and dashboard performance.

Expand/Collapse Code 
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)

n = 200_000
dates = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", "2025-11-01", freq="D")

suppliers = ["3M", "Milwaukee", "Ryobi", "LG", "Samsung", "Behr", "Husky", "DeWalt", "Delta Faucet"]
categories = ["Power Tools", "Appliances", "Paint", "Plumbing", "Smart Home", "Outdoor", "Flooring"]
merchants = ["Tools Online", "Appliances Online", "Decor Online", "Building Materials Online"]

docs.title: 2. Seasonality, Supplier Strength, and COVID Effects
docs.text:
Next, we define category level seasonality, supplier multipliers, and a function to model COVID-era demand. Premium suppliers such as Samsung and LG are assigned higher multipliers to mimic their stronger performance. Seasonal purchasing trends such as increased paint sales during warmer months are also incorporated.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# simulated seasonal patterns by month
# Multipliers try to reflect real retail + home improvement patterns
category_month_seasonality = {
    "Paint":      {1:0.6,2:0.7,3:0.9,4:1.2,5:1.35,6:1.45,7:1.4,8:1.3,9:1.1,10:1.0,11:0.85,12:0.7},
    "Power Tools":{1:1.2,2:1.0,3:1.0,4:1.1,5:1.2,6:1.3,7:1.3,8:1.2,9:1.1,10:1.1,11:1.4,12:1.6},
    "Appliances": {1:1.0,2:1.0,3:1.1,4:1.2,5:1.25,6:1.3,7:1.2,8:1.1,9:1.0,10:1.1,11:1.3,12:1.5},
    "Plumbing":   {1:0.9,2:0.9,3:1.0,4:1.05,5:1.1,6:1.1,7:1.1,8:1.0,9:1.0,10:1.05,11:1.1,12:1.1},
    "Smart Home": {1:1.1,2:1.0,3:1.0,4:1.1,5:1.15,6:1.2,7:1.2,8:1.15,9:1.1,10:1.1,11:1.3,12:1.4},
    "Outdoor":    {1:0.4,2:0.5,3:0.8,4:1.2,5:1.5,6:1.7,7:1.6,8:1.3,9:1.1,10:0.9,11:0.6,12:0.4},
    "Flooring":   {1:1.0,2:1.0,3:1.05,4:1.1,5:1.1,6:1.15,7:1.1,8:1.1,9:1.0,10:1.0,11:1.15,12:1.2},
}

# helps provide more variance in the data across suppliers
supplier_multiplier = {
    "Samsung": 3.2, "LG": 3.0,
    "Milwaukee": 2.8, "DeWalt": 2.5, "Ryobi": 2.3,
    "Behr": 1.8, "Husky": 1.3, "Delta Faucet": 1.2,
    "3M": 1.0
}

# simulating COVID shock periods (Mar 2020-Dec 2021)
def covid_multiplier(date):
    if pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01") <= date <= pd.Timestamp("2021-12-31"):
        return 1.8
    return 1.0

docs.title: 3. Sampling Base Fields and Computing Seasonality Factors
docs.text:
Here we randomly assign a date, supplier, and category to each row, then derive the corresponding seasonality and COVID multipliers.

Expand/Collapse Code 
date_col = np.random.choice(dates, n)
supplier_col = np.random.choice(suppliers, n)
category_col = np.random.choice(categories, n)

seasonal_mult = np.array([
    category_month_seasonality[c][pd.Timestamp(d).month]
    for c, d in zip(category_col, date_col)
])

covid_mult = np.array([covid_multiplier(pd.Timestamp(d)) for d in date_col])

docs.title: 4. Content Quality Segmentation and Scores
docs.text:
We segment SKUs into poor, average, and great content groups. Each group gets different distributions for content score, asset quality, bullet quality, and missing images. This will help reflect how better content usually comes with fewer issues.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# devising more variance in content scores depending on "missing images", "asset quality", and "bullet quality" - description quality
u = np.random.rand(n)
segment = np.where(u < 0.25, "poor",
        np.where(u < 0.75, "avg", "great"))

content_score = np.empty(n)
asset_quality_score = np.empty(n)
bullet_quality_score = np.empty(n)
missing_images = np.zeros(n, dtype=int)

# poor content: lower scores, many missing images
mask_poor = (segment == "poor")
content_score[mask_poor] = np.random.normal(52, 6, mask_poor.sum())
asset_quality_score[mask_poor] = np.random.normal(50, 12, mask_poor.sum())
bullet_quality_score[mask_poor] = np.random.normal(55, 8, mask_poor.sum())
missing_images[mask_poor] = np.random.binomial(1, 0.45, mask_poor.sum())

# average content
mask_avg = (segment == "avg")
content_score[mask_avg] = np.random.normal(72, 7, mask_avg.sum())
asset_quality_score[mask_avg] = np.random.normal(70, 10, mask_avg.sum())
bullet_quality_score[mask_avg] = np.random.normal(73, 7, mask_avg.sum())
missing_images[mask_avg] = np.random.binomial(1, 0.15, mask_avg.sum())

# great content
mask_great = (segment == "great")
content_score[mask_great] = np.random.normal(90, 4, mask_great.sum())
asset_quality_score[mask_great] = np.random.normal(88, 6, mask_great.sum())
bullet_quality_score[mask_great] = np.random.normal(89, 5, mask_great.sum())
missing_images[mask_great] = np.random.binomial(1, 0.05, mask_great.sum())

content_score = np.clip(content_score, 30, 100).round(1)
asset_quality_score = np.clip(asset_quality_score, 20, 100).round(1)
bullet_quality_score = np.clip(bullet_quality_score, 30, 100).round(1)

docs.title: 5. Base Traffic and Conversion Rates by Category & Supplier
docs.text:
We define base page view traffic and conversion rates per category, then apply supplier-level adjustments so stronger brands convert better.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# Different base traffic by category
base_pv_lambda = {
    "Appliances": 35,
    "Smart Home": 45,
    "Power Tools": 70,
    "Paint": 50,
    "Outdoor": 65,
    "Plumbing": 25,
    "Flooring": 30
}

# Base conversion rates by category
base_conv_rate = {
    "Appliances": 0.020,
    "Smart Home": 0.035,
    "Power Tools": 0.045,
    "Paint": 0.030,
    "Outdoor": 0.040,
    "Plumbing": 0.025,
    "Flooring": 0.028
}

# Supplier-level conversion adjustment (better brands convert better)
supplier_conv_adj = {
    "Samsung": 1.25, "LG": 1.20,
    "Milwaukee": 1.20, "DeWalt": 1.15, "Ryobi": 1.10,
    "Behr": 1.05, "Husky": 0.95, "Delta Faucet": 1.00,
    "3M": 0.90
}

docs.title: 6. Simulating Page Views
docs.text:
Page views are drawn from a Poisson distribution, where the rate (lambda) is influenced by category, seasonality, COVID effects, supplier strength, and additional lognormal noise to create spikes and a long tail. This helps create more randomness in each observation.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# page views
lambda_base = np.array([
    base_pv_lambda[cat] *
    seasonal_mult[i] *
    covid_mult[i] *
    supplier_multiplier[supplier_col[i]]
    for i, cat in enumerate(category_col)
])

# add extra randomness per row (lognormal so some SKUs spike)
lambda_noise = np.random.lognormal(mean=0.0, sigma=0.4, size=n)
lambda_final = lambda_base * lambda_noise

page_views = np.random.poisson(lambda_final).astype(int)
page_views[page_views < 0] = 0  # safety

docs.title: 7. Simulating Conversion, Orders, and Add-to-Cart Events
docs.text:
Conversion rates start from category + supplier baselines and are modified by content quality and lognormal noise. From there, we simulate orders and add to cart events.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# conversion rates vary depending on content 
conv_base = np.array([
    base_conv_rate[cat] * supplier_conv_adj[supplier_col[i]]
    for i, cat in enumerate(category_col)
])

# content impact: ~±40–50% swing based on content_score
content_factor = 1 + 0.8 * ((content_score - 70) / 30.0)
# random noise factor per row
conv_noise = np.random.lognormal(mean=0.0, sigma=0.35, size=n)

conv_rate = conv_base * content_factor * conv_noise

conv_rate = np.clip(conv_rate, 0.001, 0.25)

# binomial conversion rates
orders = np.random.binomial(np.maximum(page_views, 0), conv_rate)

atc_prob = np.clip(conv_rate * np.random.uniform(2.0, 4.0, size=n), 0.01, 0.90)
raw_atc = np.random.binomial(np.maximum(page_views - orders, 0), atc_prob)
atc_events = orders + raw_atc

docs.title: 8. Revenue Simulation Using Category-Specific AOV Ranges
docs.text:
We then estimate revenue by multiplying order counts by a randomly sampled average order value range specific to each category.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# revenue with variance per category
category_aov = {
    "Appliances": (400, 1500),
    "Smart Home": (100, 400),
    "Power Tools": (80, 300),
    "Paint": (20, 70),
    "Plumbing": (30, 120),
    "Outdoor": (50, 250),
    "Flooring": (40, 200)
}

revenue = np.array([
    orders[i] * np.random.uniform(*category_aov[category_col[i]])
    for i in range(n)
]).round(2)

docs.title: 9. Assembling the Final DataFrame
docs.text:
Finally, we assemble all metrics and metadata into a single DataFrame with SKU-level detail and other supporting fields (e.g., on time uploads, content changes, and brand review meetings).

Expand/Collapse Code 
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "event_date": date_col,
    "supplier": supplier_col,
    "brand": supplier_col,
    "category": category_col,
    "sku_id": np.random.randint(100000, 999999, n),
    "sku_name": np.random.choice([
        "Cordless Drill Kit","Smart Washer","Matte Interior Paint","Kitchen Faucet",
        "Smart Doorbell","Electric Lawnmower","Laminate Flooring",
        "Impact Driver","Mini Fridge","Exterior Paint","Shower Head"
    ], n),
    "merchant_team": np.random.choice(merchants, n),

    "page_views": page_views,
    "atc_events": atc_events,
    "orders": orders,
    "revenue": revenue,

    "content_score": content_score,
    "asset_quality_score": asset_quality_score,
    "missing_images": missing_images,
    "bullet_quality_score": bullet_quality_score,

    "on_time_upload": np.random.binomial(1, 0.85, n),
    "content_changes_made": np.random.randint(0, 20, n),
    "brand_review_meetings": np.random.randint(0, 6, n),
})

docs.title: A. Executive Summary View
docs.text:
Provides high-level KPIs and trends:

  • $265.8M revenue, 3.83% average conversion rate
  • Revenue per view, content score, missing image count
  • Multi-year revenue chart showing seasonal trends
  • Supplier leaderboard comparing revenue, revenue per view, and conversion
  • Category by supplier performance heatmap

This view highlights macro patterns and top suppliers (Samsung, LG, Milwaukee).

docs.title: B. Supplier Deep Dive View
docs.text:
Focuses on supplier efficiency and content health:

  • Revenue bar chart across top suppliers
  • Complete funnel visualization from page views → add to cart → orders
  • Image health donut chart (80% complete vs. ~20% missing)
  • Content score vs. conversion scatterplot showing strong positive trend
  • Ability to filter by supplier, category, or team to identify risk areas

This view provides clarity on which suppliers are limited by poor content and which are effective in conversion.

docs.title: C. SKU-Level Detail View
docs.text:
Highlights SKU-level variability and risk scoring:

  • Table with page views, add to cart, orders, revenue, content score
  • Flags for Critical Risk, Low Conversion, Missing Images, OK
  • Lifecycle trend showing long term page view and order patterns
  • SKU-level content score vs. conversion scatterplot to easily spot impactful items

Key findings:

  • Supplier concentration: Top three suppliers drove ~50% of total revenue.
  • Content quality impacts conversion: SKUs above content score 80 showed conversion rates 1.5-2x higher.
  • Missing images are costly: Nearly 20% of SKUs lacked images, correlating to significantly lower conversion.
  • Funnel inefficiency: Only 4-5% of page views reached orders, indicating opportunity in improving page content and clarity.
  • SKU-level risk identification: Several high traffic SKUs were flagged as Critical Risk due to poor content or asset quality.

docs.title: Business Impact (Simulated)
docs.text:
• Targeted content improvements: Identified SKUs whose content updates could drive a 10-20% lift in conversion.
  • Supplier accountability: Clear visibility into supplier content health would lead to more productive conversation with suppliers.
  • Revenue optimization: Prioritizing missing image fixes for high traffic SKUs could reclaim an estimated $8-12M in potential revenue.
  • Funnel clarity: Highlighted drop off points that guided UX and content improvements.

docs.title: Follow-Up Questions & Opportunities
docs.text:
• Can we A/B test content changes to quantify their direct impact on conversion?
  • Which suppliers consistently underperform on content compliance?
  • Are certain categories more sensitive to image quality?
  • Can we forecast future revenue using content quality as a predictor?
  • Should performance thresholds be adjusted based on category seasonality?

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Implement content A/B testing per supplier
  • Build a predictive model linking content score to conversion probability
  • Expand analysis to subcategories for more granular insights
  • Create a supplier-facing scorecard for tracking performance

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This simulated supplier analytics project showcases how simulated data can be transformed into an actionable dashboard. By analyzing performance across suppliers, categories, and SKUs, the project demonstrates how data-driven decision making can optimize merchandising strategy, supplier performance, and customer experience.

docs.title: Video Game Sales EDA (and a short history lesson)
docs.text:
Skills: Excel

Data found on: Kaggle Original data source: VGChartz

docs.title: Initial Assumptions
docs.text:
Based on my background and love for video games, I have a few assumptions I expect to see during and after performing this analysis:

  • Nintendo will be the dominant developer/publisher for a lot of years. It's impressive how Nintendo manages to never significantly change their business model or way of developing games but still continue to release popular games that appeal to a vast audience.
  • PlayStation 2 was massive. There will be a spike in the year 2000/2001 right when it was released and it will be the top console platform.
  • Grand Theft Auto: V is a timeless game released in 2013, that's still widely popular to this day. I expect to see that reflected in the data from 2013--2016, since the data set only records data until 2016 (there are points for 2017--2020 but only 4).
  • Wii Sports will have a lot of sales, maybe even the top selling game, higher than the likes of Call of Duty, GTA V, and Super Mario. Wii Sports was innovative. It was the first of its kind and brought family gaming of all ages right there into the home.
  • World of Warcraft was a revolutionary game that changed the MMO scene. I expect it to be one of the top games across the board.
  • Atari was a big contributor to the game market crash of the 1980s. I expect to see a drastic drop in sales during this time period.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Which company had the top sales?
  2. Is there a correlation between platform and sales?
  3. Which game sold the most and why?
  4. Which platform(s) are most people using?
  5. Who is publishing the most games? Does that necessarily mean they have the most sales?

Let's get right into it by first loading necessary libraries and the data set:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# libraries used
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggrepel)  
library(dlookr)
library(skimr)
library(plyr)
library(ggpubr)
library(gganimate)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(DataExplorer)
library(lubridate)

# load and view first 10 rows of data set
vgsales <- read.csv("vgsales.csv", header = TRUE)
head(vgsales)

Quick note: I reference packages throughout the code. For example, the glimpse() function will be denoted dplyr::glimpse() since it's from the dplyr package. Shoutout to Kinga on LinkedIn for this tip!

• • •

docs.title: Data Exploration
docs.text: As always, the first step should be to explore our data set and get familiar with it. One package I recently discovered and have fallen in love with for this step is the “DataExplorer” package. We’ll use this package along with a couple others to understand the data structure, find missing values, explore outliers, and visualize distributions of the data.

docs.title: Data Structure
docs.text:
Expand/Collapse Code 
# provides a summary of each column  
summary(vgsales)

# another way to get more information about each column
dplyr::glimpse(vgsales)

Just from looking at these two summaries, there are going to be “outliers”. For example, looking at Global_Sales, the median is 0.17 while the maximum value is 82.74. This is expected since we’re talking about video game sales from notable companies like Nintendo, Sony, Electronic Arts, and Activision, where there are going to be games that blow up at certain times. We can tell that the sales data is heavily right skewed by looking at the summary statistics, as there’s a wide range between the values. We’ll decide what to do with this later on (will likely perform analysis with them included regardless), but let’s move on to tidying our data set.

• • •

docs.title: Missing Values
docs.text:
When exploring the data set, I noticed 271 missing data points in “Year” and 261 in “Publisher” that had values of string “N/A” in the Year and Publisher column, as well as “Unknown” in the Publisher column. Let’s find out more using dplyr, skimr, and DataExplorer:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# replace string "N/A" with NA to use is.na() function
vgsales[vgsales == "N/A"] <- NA
vgsales[vgsales == "Unknown"] <- NA

# sum of all missing data points in each column
vgsales %>%
  dplyr::select(everything()) %>%
  dplyr::summarise_all(funs(sum(is.na(.))))

# visualize missing points by column
DataExplorer::plot_missing(vgsales)

In the context of video games, this is weird since video game release dates and publishers are usually readily available. Perhaps there was an issue with the web scraping or the original source (VGChartz) had data entry errors or a malfunction in their data collection process.

Since these data points are missing at random (MAR) and the percentage of missing observations is low relative to total observations, we could perform listwise deletion or imputation. However, I decide against it to keep the data as accurate as possible. If anyone has thoughts on this decision, feel free to leave a comment, as I’m still trying to deeply understand when to and not to use imputation. For this analysis, I performed data entry in Excel for the information I could find and loaded the new cleaned set. We’ll use this data set from here on out.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# replace string "N/A" with NA to use is.na() function
vgsales[vgsales == "N/A"] <- NA
vgsales[vgsales == "Unknown"] <- NA

# sum of all missing data points in each column
vgsales %>%
  dplyr::select(everything()) %>%
  dplyr::summarise_all(funs(sum(is.na(.))))

# visualize missing points by column
DataExplorer::plot_missing(vgsales)

Now we have much less missing observations! Let’s continue exploring the data using a few nifty R functions:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# summarize categorical variables
dlookr::diagnose_category(vgsales_clean)

Expand/Collapse Code 
# more summary statistics for each column
vgsales_skim <- vgsales_clean %>%
  skimr::skim()
data.frame(vgsales_skim)

I love the skim() function in skimr because it provides histogram sparklines so you can quickly see the distribution of numeric variables. That’s a good segue into our next data exploration topic.

• • •

docs.title: Distribution of Data
docs.text:
Firstly, let’s calculate descriptive statistics for the sales data:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# function to calculate mode. R does not have a built-in 
# function for mode like median and mean!
Mode <- function(x) {
  ux <- unique(x)
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))]
}

# get the standard deviation and mode for each sales column and store in a data frame
df_stats <- data.frame(std = c(sqrt(var(vgsales_clean$NA_Sales)), 
                              sqrt(var(vgsales_clean$EU_Sales)), sqrt(var(vgsales_clean$JP_Sales)),
                              sqrt(var(vgsales_clean$Other_Sales))), 
                      mode = c(Mode(vgsales_clean$NA_Sales), 
                                Mode(vgsales_clean$EU_Sales),
                                Mode(vgsales_clean$JP_Sales),
                                Mode(vgsales_clean$Other_Sales)))
row.names(df_stats) <- c("NA_Sales", "EU_Sales", "JP_Sales", "Other_Sales")
df_stats

Next, let’s take a look at the distribution of data by plotting histograms of each:

Expand/Collapse Code 
NA_hist <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x = NA_Sales)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(color = '#1ab5fb', bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(vgsales_clean$NA_Sales)), col = 'red', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(vgsales_clean$NA_Sales)), col = 'blue', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = Mode(vgsales_clean$NA_Sales)), col = 'green', linetype='dashed') +
  xlab("Sales in North America (in millions)") + ylab("frequency")

EU_hist <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x = EU_Sales)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(color = '#1ab5fb', bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(vgsales_clean$EU_Sales)), col = 'red', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(vgsales_clean$EU_Sales)), col = 'blue', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = Mode(vgsales_clean$EU_Sales)), col = 'green', linetype='dashed') +
  xlab("Sales in Europe (in millions)") + ylab("frequency")

JP_hist <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x = JP_Sales)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(color = '#1ab5fb', bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(vgsales_clean$JP_Sales)), col = 'red', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(vgsales_clean$JP_Sales)), col = 'blue', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = Mode(vgsales_clean$JP_Sales)), col = 'green', linetype='dashed') +
  xlab("Sales in Japan (in millions)") + ylab("frequency")

Other_hist <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x = Other_Sales)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(color = '#1ab5fb', bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(vgsales_clean$Other_Sales)), col = 'red', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(vgsales_clean$Other_Sales)), col = 'blue', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = Mode(vgsales_clean$Other_Sales)), col = 'green', linetype='dashed') +
  xlab("Sales in the rest of world (in millions)") + ylab("frequency")

# arrange the graphs into a simple dashboard
ggpubr::ggarrange(NA_hist, EU_hist, JP_hist, Other_hist)

Although this may look abnormal, it makes sense as this data represents video game sales. The gaming market is heavily saturated and most games are released into the abyss, receiving little to no traction. The sales distribution reflects that as the most frequent sales are between 0 and 2 million, with a few widely popular games creating a positive (right) skew.

• • •

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
First, I’ll create a correlation matrix using the ggcorrplot() function in the ggcorrplot library:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# create rounded matrix of sales data
correlation <- round(stats::cor(vgsales_clean[6:9]), 2)
# plot correlation matrix
ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot(correlation, outline.col = "white", type = "lower",
          ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_gray,
          colors = c("#800020", "white", "#008000"),
          lab = TRUE, lab_size = 2.5)

Let’s also visualize this using scatter plots. Note that all units for sales are in millions.

Expand/Collapse Code 
NA_EU <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x=NA_Sales, y = EU_Sales)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1ab5fb")
NA_JP <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x=NA_Sales, y = JP_Sales)) +
  geom_point(color = "#5d93fd")
NA_Other <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x=NA_Sales, y = Other_Sales)) +
  geom_point(color = "#7473fb")
EU_JP <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x=EU_Sales, y = JP_Sales)) +
  geom_point(color = "#7ed957")
EU_Other <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x=EU_Sales, y = Other_Sales)) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff66c4")
JP_Other <- ggplot(vgsales_clean, aes(x=JP_Sales, y = Other_Sales)) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff914d")

ggpubr::ggarrange(NA_EU, NA_JP, NA_Other, EU_JP, EU_Other, JP_Other)

By looking at the correlation matrix and scatter plots, we can see that NA_Sales + EU_Sales and EU_Sales + Other_Sales have the strongest positive correlation, while others like NA_Sales + JP_Sales are lower. This could be due to a multitude of reasons including, but not limited to:

  • North America and Europe are big markets with similar audiences for gaming, maybe companies market towards these two regions in similar fashions.
  • A lot of NA and EU are in the western world, which could explain similar purchasing trends.
  • Western gaming preferences are completely different from the eastern world, which can explain why NA and EU have lower correlation with Japan sales.

After all, correlation does not imply causation! Therefore, we can’t be certain by just looking at the sales data.

Correlation does not imply causation. • • •

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Now that we’ve explored the dataset and its structure, let’s get into some analysis and answer some questions! Let’s first take a look at the top 10 games at a global level:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# get top 10 games by global sales and plot them
dplyr::slice_max(vgsales_clean, n=10, order_by=vgsales_clean$Global_Sales) %>%
          ggplot(., aes(x=reorder(Name, Global_Sales), y=Global_Sales)) +
              ggplot2::geom_bar(stat="identity", fill=alpha("#1ab5fb",0.8)) +
              ggplot2::geom_text(aes(label=Publisher)) +
              ggplot2::labs(x ="Game", y = "Global_Sales (in millions)") +
              ggplot2::coord_flip()

# data frame of more detailed info for the top 10 games
dplyr::slice_max(vgsales_clean, n=10, order_by=vgsales_clean$Global_Sales)

As expected, Nintendo is dominant in this dataset which contains records from 1977 to 2016. They took every spot for the top 10 games! And Wii Sports tops the chart without competition. That really puts in to perspective how revolutionary the concept of Wii Sports was.

Another way to put Nintendo's fame into perspective is by comparing to World of Warcraft (WoW) by Activision Blizzard. In my initial assumptions, I thought WoW would be a top selling game (probably a bit of personal bias there), which it is, but Nintendo blows it out of the water. There are a few factors that may have caused this:

  • Nintendo sells on multiple different platforms while WoW is PC exclusive.
  • Nintendo has been around longer and have a bigger global reach with classic games like Super Mario Bros, Pokemon, and Tetris.
  • Personal computers (PC) had a higher barrier to entry. It was much easier and cheaper to purchase consoles, especially convenient handheld devices that Nintendo produced.
  • Let’s take a look at the top 10 when excluding Nintendo:
Expand/Collapse Code 
# filter out all rows containing Nintendo as Publisher
nint_excluded <- dplyr::filter(vgsales_clean, !Publisher %in% c("Nintendo"))

# get top 10 and visualize it
dplyr::slice_max(nint_excluded, n=10, order_by=nint_excluded$Global_Sales) %>%
          ggplot(., aes(fill=Platform, x=reorder(Name, Global_Sales), y=Global_Sales)) +
              geom_bar(stat="identity") +
              geom_text(aes(label=Publisher)) +
              labs(x ="Game", y = "Global_Sales (in millions)") +
              scale_fill_manual(values=c("#1ab5fb", "#c1ff72", "#7473fb", "#5d93fd")) +
              coord_flip()

Grand Theft Auto and Call of Duty (Modern Warfare 3 and Black Ops 2 being my personal favorites) across the board! It is crazy to think GTA V has been out for ten years and is still massively popular. Although it does seem like GTA 6 is on the horizon, where Rockstar Games tweeted in early 2022 detailing that “active development for the next entry in the series is underway”.

Also, in late 2022 a bunch of leaks came out and Rockstar tweeted to acknowledge the network intrusion which reached over 1 million likes, which really puts into perspective how massive these GTA 6 leaks were.

Back on topic, still no WoW in the top 10! This likely goes back to the point I made above about consoles being cheaper and easier to purchase. PlayStation 2 and Xbox 360 were massive and changed the game for consoles. The technical, graphical, and quality of life (QOL) jump from PlayStation 1 and Xbox was drastic and PC gaming was still a bit niche at this point since PCs were just starting to rise in the market, although growing rapidly.

PlayStation 2 and Xbox 360 were massive and changed the game for consoles.

Let’s take a look at PC games only:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# select rows containing PC in Platform column
PC_only <- vgsales_clean[is.element(vgsales_clean$Platform, c('PC')),]

# get top 10 games by global sales and plot them
dplyr::slice_max(PC_only, n=10, order_by=PC_only$Global_Sales) %>%
          ggplot(., aes(x=reorder(Name, Global_Sales), y=Global_Sales)) +
              ggplot2::geom_bar(stat="identity", fill=alpha("#7473fb",0.8)) +
              ggplot2::geom_text(aes(label=Publisher)) +
              ggplot2::labs(x ="Game", y = "Global_Sales (in millions)") +
              ggplot2::coord_flip()

# data frame of the top 10 for more detailed info
dplyr::slice_max(vgsales_clean, n=10, order_by=vgsales_clean$Global_Sales)

Wow! I knew The Sims 3 was big but did not know it sold more than WoW (no pun intended). In retrospect, it does make sense because The Sims 3 introduced a new, open world and interconnected community experience that imitated real life, which is essentially a Metaverse before the term became mainstream.

World of Warcraft: Wrath of the Lich King was my first WoW, so I’m a bit shocked that it’s not in the top 10. The story of the Lich King/Arthas was a huge attraction in the gaming world because of the character’s development from hero to anti-hero to villain. I mean who hasn’t seen that chilling, epic, unnerving cinematic trailer?

Now, let’s take a deeper look at the different platforms:

Expand/Collapse Code 
# get frequency of each platform and aggregate into a data frame
platform_freq <- plyr::count(vgsales_clean, 'Platform')
platform_sales <- aggregate(list(Global_Sales = vgsales_clean$Global_Sales), list(Platform = vgsales_clean$Platform), sum)

# top 10 platforms by frequency
dplyr::slice_max(platform_freq, n=10, order_by=freq) %>%
          ggplot(., aes(x=reorder(Platform, -freq), y=freq)) +
              ggplot2::geom_bar(stat="identity", fill=alpha("#5d93fd",0.8)) +
              ggplot2::labs(x ="Platform", y = "Frequency") +
              ggtitle("Top 10 Platforms by Frequency") +
              theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = .5))

Interesting. Nintendo DS and PS2 are closely battling for the top but how come Wii and Xbox 360 are further down? Some of the biggest games are on those platforms. It’s because we’re looking at frequency. In this case, frequency simply means the amount of games published on these platforms. Let’s look at the top 10 sales by platform:

Expand/Collapse Code 
dplyr::slice_max(platform_sales, n=10, order_by=platform_sales$Global_Sales) %>%
          ggplot(., aes(x=reorder(Platform, Global_Sales), y=Global_Sales)) +
              ggplot2::geom_bar(stat="identity", fill=alpha("#7473fb",0.8)) +
              ggplot2::labs(x ="Platform", y = "Global Sales (in millions)") +
              coord_flip() +
              ggtitle("Top 10 Platforms by Global Sales (in millions)") +
              theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = .5))

PS2 is still at the top, but now Nintendo DS has dropped and Xbox 360 has risen. While Nintendo DS had more games published on its platform, Xbox 360 had more hits that boosted sales. Now this begs the question of if there is a correlation between global sales and frequency of games published?

Expand/Collapse Code 
# merge the two previous data frames
df_platform <- merge(platform_freq, platform_sales)

# perform a simple linear model
ggplot(df_platform, aes(x=Global_Sales, y = freq)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1ab5fb") +
  geom_smooth(method='lm')

While there does appear to be some positive correlation according to the line of best fit, there's a lot of spread and distance from the line. This makes sense because publishing a lot of games on a platform does not necessarily mean the games will succeed. Although, publishing more frequently can increase the chances of releasing a popular game.

• • •

docs.title: Analysis Part 2: Time Series
docs.text:
Expand/Collapse Code 
# aggregate the sum of global_sales for each year
vgsales_global <- aggregate(list(Global_Sales = vgsales_clean$Global_Sales), 
                            list(Year = vgsales_clean$Year), sum)
ggplot(vgsales_global, aes(x=Year, y=Global_Sales, group=1)) +
  geom_line(linetype = 10, color = "darkblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1ab5fb") +
  ggtitle("Number of Global Sales by Year (in millions)") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = .5),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, size = 8))

As we can see, at the beginning of the games industry, it took some time for it to grow. Companies were still figuring out this new industry and gaming was heavily stigmatized at this point, so “normal” people were less inclined to become involved with games. Then, in the 90s hit games like DOOM, Half-Life, Pokemon Red/Blue, Crash Bandicoot, and many more came out and paved the way for gaming. In the early 2000s, we have the PlayStation 2 boom, which was a vital step in making gaming accessible and normalized in society. Consoles brought gaming to the home and became a family activity. Then in the mid 2000s-2010s, there was a major shift that made gaming a global phenomenon with the releases of Wii, Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto, Sims, Halo, and more.

The data starts to drop off after 2014 simply due to a lack of data. However, I would expect the data to stabilize in future years. While popular titles still release today, the huge increase in technological, graphical, and quality of life from the PS1 to PS2 does not occur at that level anymore simply because today’s technology has somewhat reached a peak. Games already look realistic. Performance is top-notch. Equipment and accessories are readily available. Almost every game idea has been done already.

However, we are humans and we naturally innovate towards progress. I’m sure you’ve heard it everywhere by now, but artificial intelligence (AI) has had major advancements and implementations in the real world recently. I believe AI will play a prominent role in gaming, which will create the next boost in game performance and ideas that many gamers are yearning for.

We are humans and we naturally innovate. Companies like Electronic Arts and Roblox already have been discussing the potential and plans for AI in games. • • •

Let’s have some fun with animation in gganimate by looking at some of the most well known names in the industry.

Expand/Collapse Code 
# store some of the most known publishers in a vector
top_companies <- vgsales_clean[is.element(vgsales_clean$Publisher, c('Activision', 
                                                                    'Electronic Arts', 'Nintendo', 
                                                                    'Ubisoft', 'Take Two Interactive', 
                                                                    'Sony Computer Entertainment')),]

top_companies_sales <- aggregate(top_companies$Global_Sales, by = list(top_companies$Year, 
                                                                      top_companies$Publisher), FUN = sum)
colnames(top_companies_sales)[1] <- "Year"
colnames(top_companies_sales)[2] <- "Publisher"
colnames(top_companies_sales)[3] <- "Global_Sales"

top_companies_sales %>%
mutate(label = if_else(Year == max(Year), Publisher, NA_character_)) %>%
ggplot(., aes(x=Year, y=Global_Sales, group=Publisher, color=Publisher)) +
  geom_line(size = 1, aes(color= Publisher)) +
  ggtitle("Number of Global Sales by Year (in millions)") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = .5),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, size = 8),
        legend.position = "none") +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = label), nudge_x = 1, na.rm = TRUE, size = 3) +
  gganimate::transition_reveal(as.integer(Year))

Cool stuff, right? ggplot2 is probably my favorite library in any language that I’ve used.

We can see that some of the biggest names in the industry follow a similar trend, with EA having a big jump in 2001–2003 with successful titles like Need for Speed Underground, Madden, FIFA, Medal of Honor, and more. Sony didn’t have as high sales as the rest but nevertheless still published historic franchises like Gran Turismo, Crash Bandicoot, God of War, Uncharted, LittleBigPlanet (a personal favorite), and others.

• • •

docs.title: Gaming Market Crash of the 1980s
docs.text:
One last thing I wanted to explore is the market crash of the 1980s. In the early 80s, the market was worth around $3 billion and dropped to ~$100 million by the mid-80s. It was a drastic crash that was caused by a number of factors:

  • The market was flooded with poor quality games and consoles.
  • Personal computers were starting to rise in the market.
  • Atari was the biggest at this time. Their release of E.T. was considered to be the killer of Atari and worst video game of all time, although it wasn’t the primary factor for the market crash.
  • The poor quality games made consumers lack confidence in the future of the industry.

This crash should be reflected in the data, let’s check it out.

Expand/Collapse Code 
atari_crash <- vgsales_clean[is.element(vgsales_clean$Year, c('1980', '1981', '1982', '1983', '1984', '1985', '1986', '1987', '1988', '1989', '1990')),]
atari_crash_sales <- aggregate(atari_crash$Global_Sales, by = list(atari_crash$Year, atari_crash$Publisher), FUN = sum)

colnames(atari_crash_sales)[1] <- "Year"
colnames(atari_crash_sales)[2] <- "Publisher"
colnames(atari_crash_sales)[3] <- "Global_Sales"

atari_crash_sales %>%
  mutate(label = if_else(Publisher == c("Nintendo", "Atari", "Activision"), Publisher, NA_character_)) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x=Year, y=Global_Sales, group=Publisher, color = Publisher)) +
  geom_line(size = 1, aes(color= Publisher)) +
  ggtitle("Number of Global Sales by Year (in millions)") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = .5),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, size = 7),
        legend.position = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("#a6a6a6", "green", "#a6a6a6", "orange", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#ff66c4", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6", "#a6a6a6")) +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = label), nudge_x = 1, na.rm = TRUE, size = 3.5)

As expected, we see a major crash in 1983 for Atari and an overall low point for all other publishers during the 1980s. When Nintendo shifted focus to the western world with the re2lease of the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1985, we see the sales of video games begin to revitalize. The NES had stricter quality standards for third-party developers, so the same crash that Atari saw does not happen again. Nintendo did see a dip in 1986 but bounced back with the widely successful releases of Super Mario Bros. 2 & 3, and Tetris.

Read more about the video game market crash • • •

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Phew! We’ve made it to the end. That was fun though. I hope you had as much fun as I did doing this analysis. We found out a lot of meaningful insights about video games and even learned a bit of history. If you have any questions or feedback please feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn.

Data found on: Kaggle Original data source: VGChartz
